title: The 2026 Cannabis Use Disorder Study: Read the Trend, Not Just the Headline
dek: A new national survey analysis asks how cannabis use disorder changed from 2021 to 2024. Here is what its numbers can—and cannot—tell you.
source_name: Mattingly et al., Addictive Behaviors, published August 12, 2026
facts: Researchers analyzed survey responses from 186,823 adults in repeated national samples. Estimated cannabis use disorder prevalence was 5.9% in 2021, 7.0% in 2022, 6.9% in 2023 and 7.4% in 2024. These are weighted population estimates, not diagnoses of every person who uses cannabis.
question: What does 7.4% describe?
options: The estimated share of surveyed adults meeting the study’s disorder criteria in 2024
The THC strength of a product
Everyone who used cannabis in 2024
explain: The denominator is adults in the population represented by the survey. It is not the percentage of cannabis users alone.
q2: Does this trend establish that one policy caused the increase?
o2: Yes, a trend identifies its cause
No, repeated survey observations do not by themselves establish causation
Yes, if the chart goes up
e2: Changes in use, reporting and the population may matter. A causal explanation needs additional evidence.
practice: Write down the population, years and outcome before sharing a study. If use is interfering with responsibilities or feels hard to control, speak with a qualified health professional rather than using a chart to diagnose yourself.

title: Maryland’s 2026 Cannabis Tax Numbers: Where the Revenue Comes From
dek: A dated look at the second-quarter report, with a regional chart and a quick lesson in separating tax revenue from retail sales.
facts: Maryland reported $28,685,226 in adult-use cannabis sales and use tax revenue for April–June 2026. The adult-use tax rate is 12%, following an increase from 9% on July 1, 2025. Tax receipts are not the same measure as the dollar value of all cannabis sales.
question: What does the $28.7 million figure measure?
options: All cannabis sold nationwide
Maryland adult-use cannabis tax receipts for April–June 2026
The number of customers
explain: The report concerns a specific state, tax and quarter. It is not a national sales total.
q2: What should you check before comparing two tax quarters?
o2: Whether the measurement period and tax rate are comparable
e2: A rate change or different collection period can change revenue even when buying behavior does not change in the same way.
practice: Use this chart as a reading exercise: identify the period, units and largest region. Then ask what the report does not show—individual spending, consumer safety or public-health outcomes.

title: The April 2026 Medical Cannabis Rule: What Actually Changed?
dek: Rescheduling headlines are easy to overread. Follow the published rule’s scope and keep federal status, state licensing and FDA approval separate.
source_name: Federal Register, final rule published April 28, 2026
facts: The published rule places specified FDA-approved drug products containing marijuana-derived delta-9 THC, and marijuana subject to a state medical marijuana license, in Schedule III. Its text retains other marijuana in Schedule I. This is a description of that rule’s stated scope, not a claim that every cannabis product is federally legal.
question: Which reading is consistent with the published rule?
options: Every cannabis product became legal everywhere
The rule describes specified medical categories; other marijuana is treated separately
State licensing and FDA approval became the same thing
explain: The categories and conditions matter. A headline about rescheduling cannot substitute for the actual scope.
q2: Where should you check for subsequent federal actions?
o2: The DEA’s current regulatory actions and the Federal Register
e2: Official regulatory pages give dated documents and subsequent actions. Check those before acting on an older explanation.
practice: Before sharing a policy headline, write three separate questions: Which product category? Which jurisdiction? Which effective document? Do not assume this rule authorizes interstate transport or makes a dispensary product FDA-approved.

title: Cannabis Detected Is Not the Same as Cannabis Caused: Reading CDC Data
dek: A CDC overdose report provides a useful lesson in denominators, toxicology findings and the difference between presence and cause.
facts: Among 209,166 overdose deaths in the report’s participating jurisdictions, cannabis was detected in 43,880 (21.0%) and listed as a contributing cause in 1,687 (0.8%). A toxicology finding of cannabis is not by itself a finding that cannabis caused the death. Many deaths involved other substances.
question: What does “detected” mean in this report?
options: A substance was identified; this alone does not establish causation
It was necessarily the only substance involved
It proves a retail product was contaminated
explain: Detection is a laboratory finding. Cause attribution and product contamination are different questions.
q2: What population is represented by these percentages?
o2: The overdose deaths covered by the participating jurisdictions and period
e2: The denominator is the report’s overdose deaths. It is not all cannabis users or all deaths.
practice: When two numbers appear in one headline, label each outcome and its denominator. Do not use this report to infer that a specific retail product contains fentanyl; that requires evidence about the product itself.

title: Cannabis and Heart Health: How to Read an Association
dek: A widely discussed cardiovascular study offers a practical way to distinguish an observational finding from an individual prediction.
facts: An NIH-supported analysis of survey data from nearly 435,000 adults found an association between cannabis use and cardiovascular outcomes. Its observational design does not prove cannabis caused an individual event. The study is a reason to take cardiovascular questions seriously, not a tool for calculating your personal risk from a headline.
question: What does an association establish?
options: That two measured factors occurred together in the analysis
The exact cause of every heart attack
That a product is safe for everyone
explain: An association can inform further research and clinical conversations without proving a single cause.
q2: Which next step is most useful for someone with heart-health concerns?
o2: Assume the headline predicts their personal future
Ask a clinician about their health history, medicines and cannabis use
e2: Individual health history and medications matter. A clinician can put research into that context.
practice: Prepare a clear clinical question: “I use this product by this route, and I take these medicines. What concerns should we discuss?” Bring product details, not just a strain nickname.

title: Delta-8 and Hemp Labels: Five Questions Before You Trust the Package
dek: “Hemp” is a plant-origin label, not a promise that a product is non-intoxicating, approved or free of manufacturing concerns.
source_name: FDA consumer update; historical poison-center period January 2021–February 2022
facts: FDA says delta-8 THC is psychoactive and that delta-8 products have not been evaluated or approved by FDA for safe use. Concentrated delta-8 is commonly made by chemically converting CBD, which raises manufacturing and contamination questions. “Hemp” on the front of a package does not establish that it is non-intoxicating.
question: Which claim can you safely infer from the word “hemp” alone?
options: The product cannot intoxicate
It is FDA-approved
Neither safety nor non-intoxication is established by that word alone
explain: A plant-origin or marketing label is not the same as a safety evaluation or product approval.
q2: Which information is more useful than a colorful front label?
o2: A batch identifier and verifiable testing information
e2: Traceable product details let you ask concrete questions. They still do not guarantee that a product is appropriate for you.
practice: Check ingredient identity, amount per serving, total package amount, batch number and a verifiable test report. If a seller cannot answer those questions, treat the missing information as a reason to pause.

title: CBD Approval vs. Wellness Marketing: What “Available” Does Not Tell You
dek: A product can be easy to buy without being an approved treatment. Learn how to separate an ingredient, a drug approval and a sales claim.
source_name: FDA: cannabis research and drug approval process
facts: FDA identifies one approved cannabis-derived drug, Epidiolex, and three approved synthetic cannabis-related drugs: Marinol, Syndros and Cesamet. Those approvals apply to specific drug products and uses. They do not mean that retail CBD oils, gummies or other cannabis products are approved treatments.
question: What does approval of a specific CBD drug establish?
options: Every retail CBD product has the same approval
That specific drug has an FDA approval; other products need separate evidence
Any seller may promise a cure
explain: An approval belongs to a defined drug product and its approved use, not to every product sharing an ingredient.
o2: A seller promising an unapproved product treats a disease
e2: Disease-treatment claims require evidence and appropriate regulatory authorization. Marketing confidence does not supply either.
practice: Separate three columns in your notes: the ingredient, the exact product and the claim being made. Ask whether the evidence is about this product, this use and people comparable to you.

title: Edibles, Delayed Effects and Safer Storage: A Household Checklist
dek: The packaging may resemble an ordinary snack. Clear identification and secure storage matter before anyone opens it.
facts: CDC notes that edible effects can take 30 minutes to two hours to appear and can be unpredictable. Cannabis products should be kept out of sight and reach of children and pets, ideally in secure locked storage. A delayed effect is not evidence that a product did nothing.
question: What does feeling no effect immediately tell you?
options: That taking more is always safe
That the product cannot work
Very little; edible effects may be delayed
explain: Delayed onset makes immediate judgments unreliable. This guide does not recommend a dose or a redosing schedule.
q2: Which storage choice best reduces accidental access?
o2: Secure locked storage, clearly identified and out of sight and reach
e2: A familiar food appearance can confuse other household members. Secure storage and clear identification reduce access.
practice: Audit your household: original packaging, closed container, locked location, away from ordinary snacks. In the United States, Poison Control is 1-800-222-1222; call 911 for a medical emergency.

title: Cannabis Recalls: Why the Batch Number Matters More Than the Brand
dek: A Maryland recall from September 2025 shows how to match a notice to a specific product rather than guessing from a brand name.
source_name: Maryland Cannabis Administration recall notice, September 16, 2025
facts: A September 2025 Maryland notice recalled specified Hi Color Max Chocolate Milk products after coliform testing concerns. The notice identified affected production batches and package numbers. This historical case illustrates traceability; it is not a claim that every product from the brand is recalled or that this is today’s newest notice.
question: What should you compare with a recall notice?
options: Only the brand name
The exact product and affected batch or package identifiers
The color of a shopping bag
explain: A recall can apply to particular batches. Exact identifiers are more useful than a broad brand match.
q2: What is the best source for current recall instructions?
o2: An old repost without a date
e2: Current official notices specify affected products and what to do. Follow their instructions for the product you actually have.
practice: Save a photograph of the product label and batch identifier with your receipt. If a notice matches, follow the regulator’s instructions and contact the licensed retailer; do not invent your own disposal method.

title: Cannabis Careers in Maryland: Turn an Industry Event Into a Learning Plan
dek: The state’s October 10 workforce conference highlights a broader question: which skills transfer into cultivation, processing, retail and supporting roles?
source_name: Maryland Cannabis Administration: October 10, 2026 workforce conference
facts: Maryland Cannabis Administration lists its industry workforce conference for October 10, 2026, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. at the Maryland Innovation Center in Columbia. The program includes workshops, networking and a job fair covering cultivation, processing, retail and ancillary roles. Check the official page for event updates and registration details.
question: Which preparation is most useful for exploring a role?
options: A list of transferable skills and questions about the actual work
Assuming every role involves the same tasks
Only naming favorite products
explain: Employers need role-specific skills. Inventory, customer service, quality processes and communication can matter in different ways.
q2: What does attendance at an event guarantee?
o2: Neither a job nor a license; it is a learning and networking opportunity
e2: An event can connect people and information. Hiring and licensing remain separate processes.
practice: Choose one role, identify two skills you already have and one skill to develop, and prepare a short question about daily responsibilities. After an event, record what you learned and a realistic next step.
